stories.title: $25,000 gone in 72 hours: a WhatsApp "Professor", RYDE, and every message I kept
stories.summary: Seven weeks of free tips in a WhatsApp group, then three days of exact buy orders in RYDE with screenshots for 'approval'. It crashed the day I bought the top. Then they pitched a 'compensation' trade. I lost about $25,000.
stories.body:
In September 2024, in the middle of a weekday afternoon, I typed these words into WhatsApp: "Can you explain why it happened.. all my monies were wiped out."

A day later, about $25,000 of my savings was gone. Not because of a bad trade. Because I was the target of a coordinated pump-and-dump run through a WhatsApp "stock investment group", and I kept every message. This is that story, told from my own chat history.

THE LURE: "THREE HOT TECH STOCKS"

It started in July 2024 with a WhatsApp message from a woman I'll call the "assistant". She used the name of a real, well-known venture capitalist. She offered me "three hot tech stocks" shared by a famous fund manager (another real investor's name, also misused), promised weekly returns of 15-25% and "high-yield value investments" of up to 300%, and invited me to join her WhatsApp group for free stock tips.

I joined the group that same evening. That was my first mistake, but not my last.

THE GROOMING: SEVEN WEEKS OF "FREE EDUCATION"

For the next seven weeks the group felt like a real investing community. Every morning there was a "Morning Review" of the markets. A man presented as the "Professor" posted analysis. Dozens of members, or accounts posing as members, cheered whenever a pick worked out. Nobody asked me for money. Nobody rushed me. They were building something more valuable than a quick score: trust.

Looking back, the pattern was obvious. The regulars who celebrated every win were likely shills. The "Professor" was a character. But at the time, it felt like I'd found a smart corner of the internet.

THE PLAY: RYDE, THREE DAYS IN SEPTEMBER

On a Monday in September the group announced its next "value investment": RYDE, a small Singaporean ride-hailing company listed in New York.

The pitch was elaborate. When members questioned the pick (small market value, thin trading, weak revenue, already up a lot) the "Professor" had answers ready. The chart showed "a perfect upward trend". Better yet, RYDE had supposedly agreed a strategic partnership with a big US ride-hailing company to expand across Southeast Asia, with a formal announcement coming later that month. The group's price target: $55 to $70, roughly 150-200% above where it traded. They promised we'd all sell together on the announcement day.

Meanwhile, in a private chat, the "assistant" gave me exact instructions each morning, a limit price and a number of shares. Not suggestions, instructions:

- Day one: buy at a limit of $17.40
- Day two: buy at a limit of $19.88
- Day three: buy at a limit of $21.55

Each time: set the limit order, screenshot it, and send it to her for approval before submitting. She needed to confirm I bought at the "right" price. Now I understand why: coordinated buying at set prices is what keeps a pump climbing. I was being choreographed.

And I went all in. On day two I told her: "I put all my $ here. I am not a big player. Please help me to grow." I had sold three other stocks at a loss of about $800 to free up cash. On day three I sold my Nvidia shares at a loss of about $500 and put that into RYDE too. By that afternoon I held about 1,250 shares, about $25,000 and essentially everything I had, in a single stock.

THE DUMP

That same afternoon, RYDE collapsed. My limit order filled at $21.55, near the top, and minutes later I watched it fall off a cliff. "Why RYDE is going so down now.." I asked in the group. I was told trading was halted. My savings were evaporating in real time.

Even then, they kept working me. "This is a normal sign before the rise," the "assistant" wrote. She asked for screenshots of my total holdings, again and again. She told me the company would inject $100-200 million the next morning to push the price back to $20. She said the "Professor" had now authorised margin trading, and asked how much margin I could use. On the day of the crash, they were trying to get me to borrow money to buy more.

I told her I had nothing left. "I have 0 fund."

THE EXIT

The next morning brought a final whiplash. Early on, the group's "Administrator" told everyone to hold: the price would be pushed back to $30-40. Four hours later the message flipped completely: sell everything now, because the price would fall to $0.80. The blame: "some malicious investors leaked our trading information", letting short sellers crush the stock.

I sold all of those shares, about 1,250, at 76 cents. I got back under $1,000.

Then came the second scam: the "compensation plan". The company would take "full responsibility" for my losses... by letting me join a new trade that would supposedly return 160% in three trading days. The catch: I had to put in fresh money. "I suggest you use 20k funds to participate," the "assistant" wrote. "Find a way to raise more funds." When I said I had nothing, she repeated it for hours: sell slow stocks, borrow, do whatever it takes. "This is currently the only way for you to recover all your losses."

It was the same trap, reset. They wanted the survivors to fund round two.

THE CONFRONTATION

Later that month the "assistant" came back, from a different phone number, pitching yet another "160% profit" trade. By then something had broken in me. I pushed back.

I demanded proof her group had ever made money. I told her she only ever sent instructions to buy, never to sell. I brought up an earlier stock they had pushed, which shot up and then fell back, and said plainly that I believed her people had bought low and sold into people like me. I asked why the "Professor" had shut the group down and why she was messaging from a new number.

"You made my life horrible.. i lost everything.. I can't think myself why I trusted you and sold everything to put it in RYDE."

She answered with the same script: trust was damaged, the plan would fix everything, let's rebuild the partnership. I never replied again.

THE AFTERMATH

According to public reports, the stock had run from a listing price of about $4 to a peak of $22.49, and fell by about three quarters during the day of the crash. It never recovered. Since then, investor lawsuits have been filed over RYDE's 2024 run, and they describe what I lived through: a promotion pushed through social media and chat groups, by people impersonating financial professionals. Those are allegations a court has not yet decided, but I recognised every step.

The WhatsApp group went quiet after mid-September. There were brief revivals (market commentary after the US election, more promises of future "VIP value investments") and then, in February 2025, I was simply removed from the group.

THE RED FLAGS I CAN SEE NOW

If any of this sounds familiar, please learn from my $25,000 tuition payment:

1. Borrowed famous names. The real investors whose names they used have nothing to do with WhatsApp stock tips. Scammers borrow credibility because they have none.
2. Exact buy instructions with screenshot approval. No real adviser tells you the precise limit price and number of shares, then demands proof before you submit.
3. "Don't sell" as a rule. The group forbade selling on your own. In a real community, nobody controls your sell button.
4. Pressure to put everything in one stock. I was coached to sell solid stocks (Nvidia!) and put everything into one tiny company. Spreading your money out is the opposite of what a pumper wants.
5. Fantasy fundamentals. A secret partnership, a guaranteed announcement date, a $55-70 target "in 8 working days": claims you could check, that were never checked, because they were invented.
6. The margin push on crash day. When the scheme wobbles, they don't retreat. They ask you to borrow money.
7. The "compensation" trade. The recovery pitch is the second harvest. Anyone who lost money is a proven buyer, the perfect target for round two.
8. The blame story. "Leakers" and "short sellers" caused the crash, never the people who designed it. The excuse exists to keep you from walking away.

WHAT I'M DOING ABOUT IT

I'm sharing this because silence is what these schemes count on. I've kept the complete chat history, my brokerage confirmations and the timeline. I am filing a complaint with the SEC and looking into the RYDE class action. And I started Red Flag Club so that the checks I didn't do are one tap away for anyone being pushed a stock like this.

If you lost money in RYDE in September 2024, or in any "investment group" that ran this exact playbook, you weren't unlucky. You were targeted. And there are lawyers and regulators who want to hear from you.
